The Large vesper mouse (Calomys callosus) exhibits a relatively rapid life history strategy typical of small-bodied sigmodontine rodents adapted to Neotropical savannas. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a standard thermoneutral temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C], females experience a gestational period of 21 days [tg = 21 days], a duration that falls within the typical range reported for other Calomys species. The gestation length is relatively brief compared to larger murid rodents, reflecting the accelerated developmental schedule characteristic of this genus. Birth occurs after the completion of embryogenesis, and the newborns emerge from the uterus in an altricial state. The interval between parturition and the subsequent ovulation event can be quite short, allowing females to produce multiple litters within a single breeding season. This compressed reproductive schedule is a common adaptation among small mammals occupying unpredictable or seasonally fluctuating environments, where maximizing annual output is critical for population persistence.

At birth, neonates emerge weighing approximately 2.7 grams [Wwb = approximately 2.7 grams], a modest mass that underscores the altricial condition typical of calomyscine rodents. The newborn pups are hairless and have closed eyes, entirely dependent on maternal care for thermoregulation and nutrition during the early postnatal period. This initial body mass represents a relatively small investment per offspring, consistent with a strategy that prioritizes high fecundity over per-offspring provisioning. Mothers establish lactation rapidly following parturition, providing milk that is rich in lipids and proteins to support the rapid growth trajectory of the litter. The suckling juvenile stage is characterized by a steep increase in body weight, with pups doubling their birth mass within the first week under optimal conditions. The period of dependency is relatively brief, as the species has evolved to minimize the duration of lactation in favor of more frequent reproductive events within the favorable thermal window of the summer months.

Weaning marks a critical developmental transition when the young achieve nutritional independence, and at the standard ambient temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C], this milestone occurs at 22 days since birth [tx = 22 days since birth]. The cessation of maternal milk provisioning coincides with the eruption of the pups' incisors and the development of coordinated feeding behaviors necessary for processing solid food. At this stage, the weaned juveniles are capable of independent foraging but remain vulnerable to predation and environmental stressors. Following weaning, the young enter a period of rapid somatic growth during which they accumulate body mass toward the adult asymptote. Females in particular exhibit accelerated growth trajectories to reach a body size sufficient for future reproductive effort. The weaning age of approximately 22 days is consistent with that observed in other small-bodied cricetid rodents and reflects the trade-off between maternal investment in the current litter and the female's capacity to initiate a subsequent pregnancy.

Pubertal development in females is attained within a relatively compressed timeframe, with the onset of sexual maturity recorded at 51.5 days since birth [tp = 51.5 days since birth] when the animals are maintained at the same thermoneutral condition of 36.6 °C at a temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C]. The pubertal transition is characterized by the first vaginal opening and the onset of regular estrous cyclicity, marking the female's capacity to become gravid. This early attainment of reproductive competence allows young females born early in the breeding season to contribute to population recruitment within the same year. Adult females reach an ultimate wet weight of approximately 48 grams [Wwi = approximately 48 grams], while males in the same population can attain a slightly higher asymptotic mass of 49 grams [Wwi = 49 grams], a sexual dimorphism consistent with the pattern observed in many sigmodontine rodents where males invest less in gestation and lactation. These adult body masses are typical for Calomys callosus across its distribution in the Gran Chaco and Cerrado ecoregions.

Reproductive output in this species is characterized by moderate litter sizes and a high annual frequency of breeding events. Females typically produce between 1 and 5 pups per litter [N_R_i = between 1 and 5 pups per litter], with the average litter size showing some variation depending on maternal age and nutritional condition. Under the thermoneutral conditions of 36.6 °C, the maximum reproductive rate approximates 3 litters per year [F_R_i = 3 litters per year], yielding approximately 24.7 offspring per year [Ri = approximately 24.7 offspring per year]. This high reproductive output is balanced by a relatively short lifespan, with the maximum recorded longevity in captivity reaching approximately 1.5 years [am = approximately 1.5 years] at a temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C]. The combination of early sexual maturity, short gestation, and high annual fecundity allows rapid population turnover, enabling this species to dominate disturbed habitats and agricultural landscapes across its range, a trait common among small Neotropical cricetids inhabiting seasonally variable environments.
